::: {.why}
Holding a fixed fraction is not the same as holding a fixed position, and the difference is a short volatility position you did not know you had.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Decompose the gap between a 3x leveraged ETF and three times the index return into financing, fees and rebalancing drag.
- Say in which market environment constant-leverage rebalancing helps rather than hurts, and why.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Simulate the ETF rather than trust it: from daily SPY returns, generate a synthetic 3x daily-rebalanced series and compare it against the real leveraged ETF over the same window. The tracking difference you find is fees plus financing; the gap against three times the buy-and-hold return is the rebalancing effect.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Show what drives it: run the same construction on two synthetic paths with identical start and end points, one calm and one with alternating plus and minus 5 percent days. Report the terminal value of the 3x series in both. That contrast is the whole mechanism.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Write the three-line summary into your notebook: the drag scales with variance and with the square of leverage, so it is quadratic in exactly the thing you are tempted to increase.
:::
:::
